records.title: Show HN: Coldframe, a honeypot that poses as a supermarket fridge controller
records.author: hedgerow-dev
records.storyText:
I built Coldframe, a honeypot that pretends to be a supermarket refrigeration controller. Inspired by the events on industrial fridge installations in the past weeks, I wanted to see what people would try against a convincing fake.

To learn more about this I built a honeypot that resembled perfectly the Danfoss AK-SM 800A and Dixell XWEB interfaces. Both of them are recognized on Shodan as real ones (an not as honeypots). It’s one Python file using only the standard library, and it builds on eppser/danfoss-ak-sm-decoy and public research by Synacktiv, Claroty and Ironhackers.

Things that were fun to get right:

- Matching real units. I used Shodan records of real devices to match header order, page titles, certificate fields and TLS versions. The Danfoss persona sends nginx headers in the same order as a real AK-SM 800A. The Dixell persona sends no Server header and pads its page to exactly 8,202 bytes.

- Recognising exploit attempts. It recognises CVE-2025-41450, the Danfoss “code of the day” login bypass, and records whether the submitted code is correct for today. It also tags attempts targeting three other Danfoss CVEs and the XWEB vulnerabilities.

- Letting them in. Default logins open a fake store dashboard with defrost buttons, so you see the second move, not just the first. Nothing behind it is real.

Two instances have been live for a day. So far they’ve only seen generic scanners and Shodan’s crawler, which is called refrigerator.census.shodan.io.

Feedback welcome, especially from anyone who has seen these devices in the field!

records.title: Show HN: An offline desktop companion to help maintain a healthy blink rhythm
records.author: prnysoni
records.storyText:
Profession like software engineer, mechanical / graphics designer takes a lot of strain on your eyes, observing minute details for hours and hours on screen can significantly reduce the blink rate which you might not even notice until it gets irreversibly painful, leaving you with dry eyes. I am already a victim of it, working 20 years as a research engineer in computer vision, zooming into pixel level details to hand craft algorithms. Now the doctors says its only regular use of lubricating drops can keep your eyes safe.

Now with AI and available fantastic libraries it's possible to play safe so that your body does not pay the price of your profession. EyesRhythm is build to help you keep the blink rhythm healthy by giving small audio / visual indication to maintain healthy blink rhythm not just by monitoring healthy blink rate but also keeping a watch on how rhythmic they are.

EyeRhythm also has a visual log for the neck movement. It is also capable to automatically track the face using multiple webcams that you might have on your working desk to get the best view of your eyes for accurate blink detection.

Most importantly it works completely local no internet required.

records.title: Show HN: No more code reviews. Fuzz instead
records.author: KingOfCoders
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I'm Stephan.

I'm an ex-CTO and many companies I look in today, want to get AI coded apps into production, but engineering code reviews are the new bottleneck - and engineers don't even love to do them.

No more code reviews. Fuzz instead.

appfuzz works with WASM and runs the .wasm thousands of times against a simulated backend and reports problems: crashes, n+1 queries, XSS, SQL injection, leaked secrets, blown IO/CPU/instruction budgets.

Try it of your own - you don't need an app for the demo:

https://appfuzz.dev

Why: agents write code faster than anyone can review it, and in many companies people outside engineering (marketing, sales, support) want to ship apps too - pressure from the CEO is high.

But then engineers get the pager alerts.

One way to make them safer is to treat them like iPhone/iOS apps: sandbox, permissions, app review (what appfuzz does).

It works with Wasm components in any language, Spin, wasmCloud, Fastly Compute, and Shopify Functions.

MIT. Very early state.

Which platform should I add, and what should it look for?

https://appfuzz.dev

records.title: Show HN: Jacq, a DSL that compiles model and kernel descriptions to CUDA
records.author: keithba
records.storyText:
I was working (with agents) on testing out various attention algorithm ideas I had, and I found that the existing infrastructure/libraries made it more difficult than it should be.

So I created Jacq, a DSL and compiler. A jacq file describes a model’s configuration, weights, layers, and pipeline. Jacq turns it into a standalone CUDA inference runtime and a Python weight exporter. Kernel descriptions can also generate CUDA harnesses.

The easiest way to try it is the TinyLlama example in the README. Building, validating, visualizing, and generating CUDA only require Rust. Of course, running inference does require an NVIDIA GPU, CUDA, Python dependencies, and weights. Jacq doesn't support other GPU vendors (AMD, etc) or Metal, yet (PR's welcome!)

There's also an experimental vLLM patch to compile and patch your jacq file into a vLLM build, as well.

Feedback very welcome!

records.title: Show HN: Nino – Fastest C# serializer, safe on untrusted input, also TS/Go/Rust
records.author: jnx11
records.storyText:
Nino is a source-generated binary serializer for C#, and as far as we know the fastest one. In the same BenchmarkDotNet run on GitHub runners against MemoryPack 1.21.4, it serializes classes and polymorphic types 3.5–7.2x faster and deserializes them 1.7–2.1x faster (arrays of unmanaged structs are on par). Deserializing into existing objects allocates nothing. Reproduce: https://nino.xgamedev.net/en/docs/v4/benchmarks

It is built to read bytes you do not trust: lengths are checked before allocating, depth is bounded, hash flooding is limited, and the read paths are fuzzed in CI.

The bytes are a spec, not a memory dump, so CoreCLR, Mono, IL2CPP and 32-bit hosts write the same bytes, and runtimes for TypeScript, Go and Rust pass the same conformance corpus.

Trade-offs: positional by default (VersionTolerant or Keyed for stored data), a 4-byte type id on polymorphic values, no System.Type, needs C# 9 and Roslyn 4.3+.

Docs: https://nino.xgamedev.net

records.title: Show HN: Loop – your coding agents, from your phone
records.author: jamesasefa
records.storyText:
Loop is a mobile-first companion workspace for the coding harnesses you already run. It aggregates results from your harnesses into a continuous feed that is easy to navigate and organize from your phone. I spent several months holding my newborn in one hand and trying to talk to agents one-handed on my phone. Every mobile UI is still based around chat, and it doesn’t scale on mobile, let alone one-handed!

So I built Loop: a feed of the work your coding agents do. It’s built around agent results, not chats. You can scroll your history, get notified, save outputs, search and return to conversations later. The goal is to make interacting with agents via your phone feel familiar and intuitive based on the mobile UX we’ve all come to expect.

Loop runs on your own computer — no account, no server, no app store — and pairs with your phone with one QR scan. It wraps the agents you already use (Codex, Claude Code, Pi, OpenCode, Antigravity, Muse Code, Grok Build, or any ACP agent), each keeping its own context, tools, sign-in and billing — local models through Pi or OpenCode work too.

Apache-2.0, TypeScript, SQLite. I'd love feedback from anyone else who builds from a phone.

records.title: Show HN: NLP capabilities of Opus, Astra, Argon measured by Codenames skills
records.author: daluan
records.storyText:
Hello Show HN,

I'm a college student, and I enjoy playing word games like Codenames, but it can be hard sometimes to find enough people to play when everyone is available, so I made an app that allows you to fill any seat with an AI teammate and also play against AI. This way it allows for people to get the full strategic experience of codenames just on their own.

Through this experiment, I was also able to measure and benchmark a few different LLMs through AWS Bedrock API calls and give them ELO ratings based on stuff like win rate and clue/guess accuracy. If anyone is interested, they can see more about my benchmarking methodology here: https://wordspies.com/hn#method. I think it's pretty interesting because it gives you a lot of insight into these various LLMs' NLP capabilities.

A few interesting stats were that I rated Gemini 4 Argon at 1775, GPT-6.1 Sol at 1744, GPT-6 Astra at 1723, Claude Fable 5.1 at 1623, and Claude Opus 5.5 at 1592. There are quite a few interesting things you'll find from there, like how, although newer and more expensive models tend to perform better, there are some rare exceptions, like Kimi K2.5 slightly edging out Kimi K3.

Check the site out if you're interested in NLP and data science and would like to see what level of frontier LLMs you can successfully beat!

My recipe app picked up users when a similar app shut down, and I kept noticing people scrambling to export their data, so I created this project to scratch my own itch.

The 3 main purposes this serves are:

1. Give the public a way to find how to export their data or find a replacement if one of the apps they use shuts down.

2. Give app creators a way to get their apps in front of people who are actively looking for a replacement for a similar app. Sponsored spots are labeled and never change the dates or export steps.

3. Provide inspiration for app creators looking for ideas for what to build next. Just because apps shut down doesn't mean they were not good ideas; many times they shut down for other reasons, like poor execution, no marketing, over-spending, etc.

Every date and export step links to the company's own notice.

I'm always open to ideas to make it more useful. I read all the comments and constructive criticism and input are always welcomed.

records.author: schwarztrinker
records.storyText:
I am pretty honest: there are a ton of vibecoded projects around, and I made another one... great huh?

I'm working as a data platform engineer in Germany. My day job is basically spinning up & running lakehouse platforms on US hyperscalers for SMB and some DAX companies. I mean, data engineers like to work on these platforms but since some time I really have ethical concerns about it - like: - vendor lock-in - high costs (because of cloud costs - and in most cases you are not able to connect your own metal if you have one) - non-EU vendors... - other open-source solutions have high license costs for LDAP etc. pp.

That's why is started to build my own opinionated data lakehouse platform in my spare time (tbh I also started learning agentic engineering and what harnesses are..), only curated from open source projects already available.

The building blocks are pretty straightforward imo: - Iceberg tables on whatever S3 storage you already have - Trino for SQL and Spark Connect for jobs - Airflow for schedules, plus notebooks, Kafka streams and dashboards - One web UI and one API over all of it - stuff around like OIDC, secrets management etc.

It's fully pre-alpha. But I want to use it as an internal pitch project at my current employer to push agentic engineering & the idea of creating our own data platform for our non-hyperscaler customers.

Site: https://stardelt.io Code: https://github.com/stardelt

I'm happy to hear what you think about it :)

Cheers, Martin

records.title: Show HN: Sentient, Your Coding Agent Shouldn't Be a Black Box
records.author: epynonymous
records.storyText:
after working quite rigorously for a few months with claude code, I found out that I was blindly approving permission requests for the sake of progressing my projects, this led me to realize that coding agents generate hundreds of commands underneath the covers which is necessary, but quite scary if you ask me. you've probably seen news recently about agents deleting databases or environments in production by accident. so i wanted to create something to gain visibility into what's actually happening and potentially block things before they occur.

coding agents often log everything that they're doing, but even still, i want the ground level truth of what's happening. that's why i created sentient, written using claude code. it's open source (mit license), runs completely locally, no cloud syncing, read only, and watches actions straight from the kernel. all of this is summarized with a hopefully simple web ui.

i run claude code on linux, so kernel tracking relies on tetragon, but, at the same time, i am trying to get approval to use security endpoint on mac, and will eventually roll out on windows. if you want to run sentient today against just the agent logs without kernel logs, that's also available now, you just need golang and sqlite3 to build. and today, i'm only supporting claude code, but will eventually get to codex and the like. please have a try, ping me if you have any questions or comments: hello@nosaka.ai

https://github.com/nosaka4i/sentient

https://nosaka.ai/blog/sentient

records.title: Show HN: Browser extension shows where to buy current domain name
records.author: timbowhite
records.storyText:
Domain Hunter finds if and where you can buy the current domain name loaded in the browser.

Or if you're searching for a domain name on a registrar/aftermarket, it auto-detects the searched domain and finds the best prices.

It uses the domain inventory data aggregated by DomDB.com. And shows other info like registered extensions, keywords, DNS records, etc.

No domain lookups are ever logged - only IP addresses are logged to prevent abuse, which are deleted after 2 weeks.

Website: https://domdb.com/tools/browser-extension

Chrome: https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/domain-hunter/hhpdn...

Firefox: https://addons.mozilla.org/en-US/firefox/addon/domain-hunter...

MS Edge: https://microsoftedge.microsoft.com/addons/detail/domain-hun...

Video: https://youtube.com/shorts/y2kWP2oEl2k

records.title: Show HN: I built a free trivia hosting app with no accounts or subscriptions
records.author: thepolymoth
records.storyText:
It's basically a fancy wrapper around your quiz data so that as a host you can show showmanship and present like a TV show host. Built exclusively for the use case of live quiz/trivia hosting with friends and family, in person or over zoom. 
Few features I always lacked and few problems with other alternatives that this web app solves:
1. Keeping costs low or free since most apps require a subscription, and much like geoguessr, I don't want to pay a monthly fee for something I may use very occasionally. Since I don't store any data and it remains in local browser storage, no need for accounts/auth and cloud storage (of-course there were trade-offs)
2. Doing buzzer rounds or audio/video clues that previously required using different apps. 
3. Friction of making accounts or downloading apps. This works completely in browser using laptop and phones.
4. As a quiz master or host, I don't like being tied to my laptop when hosting, so I made a quiz master remote where I can control the entire quiz using my phone and move around freely.
